orchestrator_causes: Customers genuinely cannot distinguish quality from fakes at the point of sale, so the problem is an information gap — buyers have no credible signal to justify paying more before the product fails.

Even customers who understand the quality difference cannot afford 1.5–3 million shillings upfront, so the problem is affordability and cash flow, not perception — they choose the cheap option because it is the only one within reach.

The repeated failures of fake products have poisoned trust in the entire solar category, so the problem is that the whole market's demand is collapsing regardless of what any individual seller does about price, information, or payment terms.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** Your own words say it clearly. "Customers cannot tell the difference until it stops working," and "on the surface the panels look the same." The buyer standing in front of you has no way to see that your system is better, so from where they stand, you just look like a more expensive version of the exact same thing. That is why they feel you are overcharging.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the real problem, you should see that customers who fully understand the quality difference (maybe an engineer, or someone whose neighbor's cheap system already failed) rarely argue about your price. The price complaints come mostly from first-time buyers who have nothing to compare against.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be giving buyers a credible signal they can check before paying. Show them working systems you installed years ago, connect them to past customers who can vouch for you, and put your warranty in writing with clear terms so quality becomes something they can verify, not just trust.

The previous advisor assumes that if customers just understood the quality, they would buy, but understanding does not fill an empty wallet.

**CAUSE:** The real block is money, not perception. A full system costs 1.5 to 3 million shillings upfront, and most of your customers (households in poor areas, small shops, upcountry builders) simply do not have that cash lying around. Even a customer who fully believes your system is better will still pick the cheap one, because it is the only thing they can actually afford today. You said it yourself when you started thinking about installments so "the higher price feels manageable."

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you should see customers nod and agree your system is better, and still walk away to buy cheap, saying something like "I will come back when I have the money." The objection is about timing and cash, not doubt.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be building a real pay-over-time plan through mobile money, with a small deposit and monthly payments, so people can start with the quality system now instead of saving up for years.

Both previous advisors treat this as a one-customer-at-a-time problem, one about proof, the other about cash. But the entrepreneur told us the damage is bigger than any single sale, and neither reading takes that seriously.

**CAUSE:** You said it plainly. "They buy the cheap one, it fails in a year, and then they distrust all solar including mine, so I lose the whole market not just one sale." The fakes are not just underpricing you, they are burning the reputation of solar itself, so people who got burned (or watched a neighbor get burned) now believe all solar is a scam. That means your problem is a shrinking pool of people willing to consider solar at all, no matter your proof or payment terms.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice fewer people even calling to ask about solar over time, and new leads opening with suspicion like "does this one also die after a year?"

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be rebuilding trust in the category publicly, organize with other honest installers, get visible working systems in each community, and let satisfied neighbors become your proof.

The faults surface after sale because his testing process cannot detect latent failures like degrading batteries or dying drives in a quick check, so the problem is inadequate pre-sale diagnostics, not the source or customer expectations.

Customers come back angry demanding refunds because he sells used machines with no upfront agreement about their used nature and no guarantee, so the problem is unmanaged customer expectations, not the actual fault rate.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** The real trouble starts before the laptops even reach your shop. You said yourself the machines "arrive with hidden faults like bad batteries or failing hard drives," and that many dealers in your building buy "from the same import sources." That tells me your supplier is sending you low-grade stock, so no amount of testing or warranty on your end fixes a problem that begins upstream.

**PREDICTION:** If this is correct, you should see the same kinds of faults (weak batteries, dying hard drives) showing up again and again across many machines from the same shipment, and other dealers buying from that source should be facing the exact same complaints.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be finding a better importer, even at higher cost, and testing them with a small trial batch first. Track the fault rate of that batch against your current supplier so you can prove which source gives you cleaner machines before committing more money.

orchestrator_causes: The entrepreneur genuinely loses sales because power and network outages physically prevent service delivery during peak demand, so the problem is infrastructure reliability that backup equipment would directly solve.

Customers leave during outages because they have no reason to wait or return — competitors nearby offer identical services — so the real problem is the entrepreneur's lack of differentiation or customer loyalty, not the outages themselves.

The infrastructure will keep failing regardless of backups, and the truly protected revenue is the form-filling expertise people cannot self-serve, so the real problem is over-reliance on commoditized, outage-dependent services rather than building around defensible skills.
raw_diagnoses:
**CAUSE:** You told me plainly that your biggest problem is the unreliable internet and power in Lira. When the power goes off or the network is down, you cannot print or help anyone, and customers with urgent deadline applications get angry and leave. This is not a customer problem or a pricing problem, it is a straight infrastructure failure that stops you from delivering the service right when demand is highest.

**PREDICTION:** If this is the real problem, you should see that the customers you lose almost always leave during a specific power cut or network drop, not on days when everything is running smoothly. On good days your busy moments should convert into sales without complaints.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be buying the backup power (solar or small generator) and a second network SIM, starting with whichever fails more often. Track for two weeks how many sales you lose to outages, then compare that lost income against the equipment cost to confirm it pays for itself.

The previous advisor treats the outage as the whole story, but misses that customers only bolt because you offer nothing they cannot get from the shop next door.

**CAUSE:** You said yourself there are "a few other printing shops in Lira offering the same services," so when your power or network drops, customers have zero reason to wait for you. If you were the only one who could fill their government forms well, or if they trusted you above the rest, they would come back in an hour instead of walking to a competitor. The outage is just the moment that exposes how easily replaceable you feel to them.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you should see that even on good days with full power, customers often go wherever is closest or cheapest, and few ask for you by name or return as regulars.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be building loyalty so people wait for you, offer a "come back when power returns" hold on their job, take their number, and make your form-filling service something only you do reliably well.

Both previous advisors get stuck on the same trap. The first thinks buying backups solves it, and the second thinks loyalty solves it, but neither asks why you are betting your business on services (printing, copying, browsing) that die the moment the power or network dies.

**CAUSE:** Look at what you told me. Printing, copying, and browsing all stop dead when infrastructure fails, and browsing customers are already shrinking as more people get smartphones. But you also said the form-filling "earns well because people cannot do it themselves." That skill is the one thing outages and competitors cannot easily copy, yet you treat it as a side service instead of your core.

**PREDICTION:** If this is right, you will notice the form-filling customers are more patient and willing to come back later, while the print and browse customers are the ones who storm off during an outage.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be growing the form-filling expertise into your main offer (learn every government portal, application type, and deadline better than anyone), so your income leans on your skill rather than on machines that keep failing.
